It's not unique. I for one agree. Mathematics is obfuscated because mathematicians prioritize compactness on the page over ease of understanding. This results in confusing notation (single-character variable names, implicit multiplication, implicit parentheses) and large numbers of omitted steps.

If I want to understand some mathematics, my first step is always translating it to code. Modern code (excluding array languages) no longer has a culture of minimizing character count, and omitting "obvious" steps is not possible. LLMs are based on an architecture (transformers) that was originally designed for natural language translation, so it doesn't surprise me that they're good at this.

children.author: remus
children.text: While I think there is some truth to this I think the framing is very uncharitable. The obscurity in maths comes from layers upon layers of abstraction because this is a useful way for humans to work with these complex ideas. I think we see some of this with these proofs that have been translated to lean: some of the proofs are millions of lines of lean, imagine trying to wrap your head around a codebase that is millions of lines! And just for a single proof!  These impenetrable abstractions that mathematicians have created are like a mental model for a massive code base.

This is my hypothesis too. I work with LLMs daily. I use frontier models all the time, and I work in a startup that trains its own special-purpose models. At no point in the course of my work do I see anything resembling superhuman intelligence. I see superhuman stupidity, ie. stupidity so extreme that it exceeds what any human is capable of by orders of magnitude. So where are the superhuman math results coming from? Simple: translation. I've already thought this for a long time, that math is an obsfucated field and that programming already makes it far simpler to understand. So you train a machine to throw tons of compute at translating math into programming, and blow the field out of the water because it's effectively been deobfuscated. Math proofs had a sort of security by obscurity; they were not genuinely supremely difficult, but rather very few people worldwide worked on them and their work was heavily obscured, so the great deobfuscation machine comes along and trivialises that aspect and suddenly the facade crumbles. I think all of this could have been achieved a long time ago had humans done the deobfuscation, but there wasn't sufficient programming <--> maths cross-domain expertise or financial incentive to develop it.

children.author: black_knight
children.text:
I have hear people make this comparison many times, but it just does not hold up under scrutiny.

I think the confusion stems from people being exposed to set theory, believing that formalisation is akin to writing those horrible set encodings of everything. Which I would agree would be akin to writing assembly.

But Lean, Rocq and Agda are all based in type theory. Which means it is more like the highest level programming language you can imagine! You have all the powers of abstraction, but you still have to convince the type checker – i.e. no “trust me, bro” casting, or even questionable while loops (“I promise this loop finishes at some point”).

These abstractions along with meta programming techniques (“tactics”) means that you can write readable correct proofs, but it takes effort. Math is extremely deep, and getting formalised all the way to the research frontier in a given subfield is a serious undertaking.

i feel like this would be the equivalent of having all CS undergrads program with assembly and assembly only.

it might(?) work? but abstractions exist for a reason (mostly...)

I am a math undergrad and I tried lean. It probably is because of habit and familiarity but I still find lean proofs harder to read than NL proofs. I wonder what if the math education switch entirely to a formal language (not necessarily Lean) will be?

> Suppose lean in its current state existed 15 years ago, and suppose the math community eagerly started contributing en masse to a shared repository of code. How much of the breakthroughs and longstanding questions in mathematics that we’ve seen answered this year do you think we would have solved?

(Former grad student in math here who has spent whole weeks formalizing in Lean lemmas that would be considered by professional mathematicians writing a mathematics text / paper as obvious ("without loss of generality we can assume that....", "it should be clear that...")

Probably very few or none.

These systems (mostly) don't help you discover new mathematics. They are a tool for formalization.

It just turns out that combining them with LLMs is the secret sauce. LLMs have quite a bit of creativity but make a lot of mistakes. The Lean typechecker never makes a mistake but has no creativity. Get them to work together in an iterative loop and you get what we have now.

children.text: OpenAI having NL proofs earlier than Lean ones would require trust in the proof without ability to check it automatically. Perhaps Lean proofs are published later because it is considered a less important implementation detail or because there is a cleanup step that takes time.

> Suppose lean in its current state existed 15 years ago, and suppose the math community eagerly started contributing en masse to a shared repository of code. How much of the breakthroughs and longstanding questions in mathematics that we’ve seen answered this year do you think we would have solved?

Absolutely none of them. I have some experience formalizing math by hand in the pre-LLM era. I never started with making the formal proof. It is way too difficult. I don't think I've ever heard of any mathematician starting with a formal proof vs writing a natural language proof. Starting with a formal proof vs a natural language proof is putting the cart before the horse.

Without a natural language proof, or at least an idea of how to write the natural language proof, it is very difficult to write a formal proof. It's flying blind. I can blindly apply tactics, but without some larger plan to guide my formal proof, it's near impossible to make progress on all but the most trivial proofs. I don't think it has ever happened that a major proof was formalized before its natural language proof was written.

I don't think people appreciate just how labor-intensive it previously was to write a formal proof. It takes easily 10-1000x as much time for a human to write a formal proof vs a natural language proof. Even just formalizing a single undergraduate math textbook for certain subjects by hand was considered a multi-year project for a professional mathematician to undertake.

Formalizing a new paper, even if it was building on previously already formalized theorems, could be months of work just by itself, even with the natural language proof in hand.

It is no surprise that OpenAI releases natural language proofs before they release formal proofs. Presumably the same difficulty difference applies to LLMs as well.

children.author: rakejake
children.text:
This is a great question. I am not a mathematician but I've had similar questions about my own field (CS/Elec) as well.

I have always felt that a huge amount of brain power has to be expended in understanding the jargon and getting used to the machinery. Once we get past that, what people would think are highly challenging subjects become rather simple and logical. An analogy I like to use is old people struggling with simple tech tasks. I remember an uncle of mine who approached me to fix their laptop which wasn't connecting to the internet. Turns out the laptop had not been booted in a while and the public certs shipped with the machine had expired. Said person is a highly accomplished person in their field but was helpless when it came to this task. After I solved the issue, the uncle was eager to know what the problem was and I tried to ELI5 it but to no avail. It is possible I did a really bad job of explaining it but there was too much basic machinery to cover. Why is there a public and private key, what is symmetric/asymmetric, why do certs even expire etc. I couldn't even touch on the foundational math underpinning all of it so I left him in a confused daze.

To any SWE, all this is table stakes but for non-tech people it is way too much jargon. Today, I'm confident my uncle could prompt his way to a working understanding of PKI - heck maybe even some aspects of cryptography and prime number math that makes it work. This is where I see LLMs making a massive difference - they can crunch a massive amount of jargon and leave only the actual trick/idea for you to understand.

This is also what people like Szegedy and Tao have also said - LLMs will make math closer to what SWE is - a lot more people doing it in workmanlike fashion rather than a small community writing papers. At one point, dynamic programming was some research topic that Bellman worked on and now every 20 year old works on tens to hundreds of these problems in the hopes of cracking a job. But I'm sure the Math field will go through some turbulence and I wish them the best. There will always be a need for SMEs who deeply understand a subject and can come up with interesting problems.

children.author: Gigachad
children.text:
I remember attending a talk about Lean well before LLMs or the current AI craze. They were trying to automate mathematics for a long time.

While everything seems crazy right now, the building blocks have been coming together for a long time now.

Suppose lean in its current state existed 15 years ago, and suppose the math community eagerly started contributing en masse to a shared repository of code. How much of the breakthroughs and longstanding questions in mathematics that we’ve seen answered this year do you think we would have solved?

In other words, how much of the developments this year are directly attributable to LLMs using lean, versus lean just being a significantly more productive language for some subset of mathematics compared to English and LaTeX?

Given how much we’ve seen formalized this year it feels hard to believe that this couldn’t have happened earlier.

Follow up question: do you think mathematicians would be as upset about the rapid changes in their field if they were the result of a collective shared effort on github, authored entirely by humans who all share the credit, versus that same outcome but authored by a large language model?

In other words, are the mathematicians upset about large language models, or are they really just upset that formalization and massive collaboration have turned out to be highly effective and has negated the heroic angle that mathematicians previously enjoyed, thinking in a locked room by themselves?

Food for thought.

A coworker recently remarked that lean seems like a new foundational language family that every programmer should be able to read, on par with C and Python, and I think it’s pretty hard to disagree with that. Next generations of models are going to be RL’d on Lean more and more because it pays dividends in winning the math war against their competitors, and this will benefit users of lean not only for mathematics but also as a general programming language and as a vehicle for other DSLs. For example, I think Sparkle (a Lean based HDL) or something like it makes a lot of sense in 2026 and beyond.

They created an implementation of a Lean kernel in Lean (con-leche) and verified it as consistent.

Since there can be bugs in its compiler and runtime, they translated the code into Rust (con-ron), and verified the resulting kernel with another Rust-based verification tool.

There is also an ongoing verification project of Lean4, which is written in Lean4 itself. (My mental model is Lean4 := Raku and Lean := Perl)

So we have two verified kernels now, and another is awaiting release.
